title: Here am I (Isaiah 6:1–8)
hook: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, and says here am I, send me

segments.voice: Yesterday, we began the prophets with the word prophet, and your line was truth to power. Did you hear an uncomfortable truth without arguing back? Day four hundred sixty-three.

It begins with a date: "In the year that king Uzziah died." A king is dead, and a whole kingdom is waiting to see what comes next. In that year, a man named Isaiah is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and he sees something. The Lord, sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the hem of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him, beings with six wings each, calling to one another. The doorposts shake. The house fills with smoke. Today, the moment Isaiah is called, and the two words he answers with.
screen: `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.` → `A THRONE, HIGH AND LIFTED UP.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: The text calls these beings seraphim, a name some readers link to a Hebrew word for burning. They cover their faces with two wings, their feet with two, and fly with two, and they call: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Churches still sing that line in the Sanctus at communion, and in hymns. And here is Isaiah's first reaction. Not wonder. Terror. "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips." He doesn't say he's done terrible things. He says his mouth is unclean, the very thing a prophet needs. Then one of the seraphim flies to the altar, takes a live coal with tongs, and touches it to his lips. Your guilt is taken away, it says. And now, at last, a question from the throne. Notice it isn't a command. "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" And Isaiah: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew that's hineni, one short word: here I am. It's what Abraham says when God calls him, what Moses says at the burning bush, what the boy Samuel says in the night. It doesn't mean I'm qualified. Isaiah has just said he isn't. It means I'm present, I'm listening, I'm available. And it comes before he knows the job. The next verses give him a hard message for a people who won't listen. He says yes first. Christians hear their own calls in this scene at ordinations and at sendings for mission, and in ordinary moments too: someone asks who will go, and a hand goes up.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME: UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A LIVE COAL ON THE MOUTH.` · `HINENI: HERE I AM.` · then, large: `HERE AM I; SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say here am I. Settle, and breathe. Notice where you are right now: the chair, the room, the sounds, the light. Let yourself be fully here, the way the word hineni means. Then think of one place this week where someone is asking, in their own way, who will go: a neighbor, a coworker, a family member, a cause. You don't have to fix it. Just turn toward it. If you pray, you can say Isaiah's words: here am I; send me. If you don't, simply say here I am, and mean it. The bell holds the time.
Here am I. Hineni in Hebrew: present and available, the answer of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah, said before knowing the job.
Your line: send me. Today, when someone asks for a volunteer, a hand, or just a listener, try saying it out loud: here I am. Day four hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Christians sing the seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' in the Sanctus of the communion service, and Isaiah 6 is often read at ordinations and when people are commissioned for mission or service.

fork.setup: you've just seen the Lord on a throne and felt your own unworthiness. a voice asks: whom shall I send? what do you say?

fork.reveal: Isaiah says "here am I; send me," right after saying he's a man of unclean lips. he answers before he knows the job.

original.note: Hebrew: here I am. one word, said by Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah when called.

trapdoor: what you thought: here am I means I'm ready because I'm good enough.
what it means: I'm present and available, said by someone who has just confessed he isn't worthy.
what a scholar hears: hineni, a single word of readiness. the seraphim's threefold holy lives on in the Sanctus, and the call is dated by a king's death, not by a calendar year.

notes: Uzziah reigned 52 years (2 Kings 15:2; 2 Chronicles 26:3); 'about fifty years' in the voice. His death is commonly dated c. 740 BC (estimates vary c. 742–733). Confirm.
Hineni: Genesis 22:1, Exodus 3:4, 1 Samuel 3:4 all use hineni (in Samuel, 'Here am I'). Confirm.

'Whom shall I send' quoted in voice: KJV 6:8 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' is part of the verse; the source lists only 'Here am I; send me.' — the question also appears verbatim. Confirm.
'Isaiah's book opens the prophets in the Christian Bible' (the Latter Prophets also begin with Isaiah in the Hebrew Bible, after the Former Prophets). Confirm phrasing.
